question: Can a fixed residual architecture be shortened for a target image dataset by progressively activating blocks until a user-selected accuracy threshold is met, while retaining nearly all full-depth accuracy?

key_findings.claim: The method searches only along a fixed prefix-depth axis: it warms every depth briefly, restores the warmed checkpoint when a new prefix is activated, and stops when validation accuracy reaches a user-specified target.
key_findings.evidence: ResNet-18 is partitioned into eight residual blocks and ResNet-34/50 into sixteen; every prefix receives a separate output head. Algorithm 1 warms the full parameter set, starts from an initial prefix, declares convergence after 23 epochs without improved accuracy, appends a block, reloads the warm-up state, and returns once the target is reached.

key_findings.claim: The reported compact models stay within one percentage point of their separately reported full-depth accuracies while reducing stored parameters by 73.06% to 98.64% across five dataset/architecture pairs.
key_findings.evidence: Table I reports MNIST ResNet-18 at 2/8 blocks, 0.61 MB, and 99.31% versus 44.78 MB and 99.61%; EMNIST at 3/8 and 95.04% versus 95.17%; SVHN ResNet-34 at 5/16 and 96.08% versus 96.51%; Fashion-MNIST at 6/16 and 93.54% versus 94.52%; and CIFAR-10 ResNet-50 at 11/16 and 94.12% versus 95.01%.

key_findings.claim: The experiment does not isolate progressive expansion from ordinary depth selection, so it cannot show that the proposed search is better than training the winning shallow prefix directly.
key_findings.evidence: Table I compares the selected prefix only with the full-depth model. There is no independently trained same-depth baseline, no exhaustive depth sweep, no random or successive-halving search, and no ablation of warm-up, checkpoint restoration, separate heads, or progressive ordering. Figure 4 only contrasts a warm-up/no-warm-up curve for one dataset without numerical uncertainty.

key_findings.claim: The paper's efficiency claim is a deployment-size result, not a demonstrated search-cost reduction.
key_findings.evidence: The procedure first warms all depth levels and then trains successive prefixes to convergence, but reports neither cumulative search FLOPs, wall time, energy, nor comparison against NAS or a direct grid. Table I reports inference FLOPs and model size only after selection; its claimed savings therefore do not account for the one-time search.

key_findings.claim: Calling the returned prefix an 'optimal depth' is not justified by the stopping rule: it is merely the first tested prefix to cross a chosen accuracy threshold under one training path.
key_findings.evidence: The objective is not a joint accuracy-cost optimization and the algorithm does not compare every feasible depth after converged independent training. Its result depends on initial depth, threshold, patience, warm-up checkpoint, depth order, and stochastic optimization; a later or separately trained shallower model could dominate it.

key_findings.claim: The evidence is confined to small image-classification benchmarks and a different backbone for different datasets, leaving transfer and task-complexity claims untested.
key_findings.evidence: Only five 10- or 26-class datasets are evaluated, and the pairing changes from ResNet-18 to ResNet-34 to ResNet-50. No ImageNet-scale task, non-vision domain, repeated seed, uncertainty interval, latency measurement, device measurement, calibration test, or cross-dataset reuse of a selected depth is reported.

method.core_idea: Treat prefix depth in a preselected residual network as a one-dimensional capacity search and grow the active prefix only when the current prefix has converged without reaching a target validation accuracy.
method.mechanism: Partition a ResNet into residual-block prefixes, attach an output head to each prefix, warm the entire network at a small learning rate, then train the shallowest selected prefix. After a patience counter reaches 23 epochs without improvement, append one block and reload its parameters from the warm-up checkpoint. Stop at the first prefix reaching the target, copy that prefix and its head, and fine-tune it for deployment.
assumptions: Prefix depth is a useful monotone proxy for task capacity and later blocks can be removed without needing a different topology.
A user can select an accuracy target that meaningfully represents the desired performance-efficiency trade-off.
Warm-up gives every later prefix a fair initialization even though prefixes share upstream parameters and use separate heads.
Validation accuracy and convergence detection are stable enough that one stochastic training trajectory selects a reproducible depth.
Inference FLOPs and serialized float32 parameter size are adequate proxies for device latency, memory, and energy.
The chosen small image benchmarks represent the broader low-complexity tasks motivating the method.

techniques.role: Defines a nested family of residual subnetworks by progressively including residual blocks.
Provides a classifier at every candidate depth so each active prefix can be trained and evaluated.
Initializes all blocks before any later block is activated in the progressive search.
Adds a block after 23 non-improving epochs and stops at the first target-accuracy crossing.
Retrains the extracted prefix without changing its selected depth.

evaluations.metric: Accuracy, float32 model size, and FLOPs
evaluations.result: The selected 2/8-block prefix reports 99.31% accuracy, 0.61 MB, and 117.36M FLOPs versus 99.61%, 44.78 MB, and 458.21M for full depth.
evaluations.baseline: A separately reported full-depth ResNet-18; no independently trained 2-block control.

evaluations.result: The 3/8-block prefix reports 95.04% accuracy and a 96.54% size reduction.
evaluations.baseline: Full-depth ResNet-18 at 95.17%; no seed distribution or equal-depth baseline.

evaluations.result: The selected 5/16 and 6/16 prefixes report 96.08% and 93.54% accuracy with 96.44% and 95.04% size reductions.
evaluations.baseline: Full-depth ResNet-34 at 96.51% and 94.52%; no pruning, OFA, slimmable, or direct-search baselines.

evaluations.result: The 11/16-block prefix reports 94.12%, 25.44 MB, and 906.19M FLOPs versus 95.01%, 94.43 MB, and 1315.02M at full depth.
evaluations.baseline: Full-depth ResNet-50; no comparison with a CIFAR-sized architecture or independently trained shallow ResNet.

evaluations.result: Figure 4 visually attributes smoother, faster convergence to warm-up.
evaluations.baseline: A no-warm-up curve without numeric time-to-target, repeated seeds, or uncertainty.

limitations: [Author-visible scope] The search changes only prefix depth inside ResNet-18/34/50; widths, kernels, block types, resolution, and non-prefix selections are fixed.

[Reviewer-identified] The method is not compared with training each depth independently, simple grid search, pruning, stochastic depth, LayerDrop, slimmable/OFA networks, early exits, or contemporary hardware-aware NAS.
[Reviewer-identified] Search cost is not reported, although multiple prefixes are trained to convergence after an all-depth warm-up.
[Reviewer-identified] Results lack seeds, confidence intervals, validation/test split details, target thresholds by task, training-epoch totals, and hardware measurements.

[Reviewer-identified] The selected network can be almost as accurate as full depth by construction because the stopping threshold tolerates a chosen loss; the frontier at other tolerances is not shown.
[Reviewer-identified] Five small image datasets do not establish that selected depth tracks an intrinsic dataset complexity or transfers to similar datasets.
[Reviewer-identified] Accuracy and FLOP/parameter counts do not establish real edge-device latency, peak activation memory, energy, or throughput.
failure_modes: A noisy validation improvement can reset or trigger the patience counter and select a different prefix across seeds.
A shallower prefix may learn more slowly but eventually dominate; first-crossing selection can incorrectly grow past it.
Reloading every newly activated prefix from the original warm-up state can discard useful co-adaptation from the current shallower trajectory.
Separate output heads add parameters during search and may give unequal optimization quality across depths.
Tasks needing high-level receptive fields can make prefix accuracy non-monotone or require redesigned downsampling rather than merely more blocks.
FLOP reductions may not translate to device speed when kernels become small, memory-bound, or poorly optimized.
Validation-driven target selection can leak repeated validation decisions and overfit the selected depth.
reusable_insights: A nested prefix family turns architecture selection into an inexpensive-to-describe one-dimensional decision, which is useful when topology flexibility is less important than predictable deployment.
A genuine depth-selection study should separate the quality of the selected subnetwork from the cost and bias of the search trajectory.
Prospective selection rules need an explicit objective and a held-out test of whether the selected candidate lies on the independently trained Pareto frontier.

For generated RL environments, the analogue is to stop increasing environment complexity only after a prospective learner-independent signal crosses a threshold, then verify the chosen environment against independently trained agents and budgets.
open_questions: Does progressive expansion select the same depth as an exhaustive, independently trained sweep, and at what cumulative search cost?
How stable are selected depths across random seeds, target thresholds, patience settings, data subsets, and distribution shifts?
Can a multi-objective rule replace the arbitrary accuracy target and recover a calibrated latency-accuracy Pareto frontier on actual devices?
Does a depth selected on one dataset transfer to another dataset claimed to have similar complexity?
Would stochastic-depth, LayerDrop, OFA, or slimmable training produce better reusable subnetworks under the same compute budget?
Can the method extend beyond prefix removal to preserve stage transitions, receptive field, and feature resolution when very shallow networks are selected?

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Networks with Stochastic Depth
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct prior work on training residual networks at varying effective depths.
competitive_landscape.difference: Stochastic depth samples residual-layer bypasses during training and uses the full network at test time, primarily regularizing and shortening training paths. ODN instead follows one deterministic prefix-growth path and deploys the first target-crossing prefix, but does not compare against this established variable-depth training control.

competitive_landscape.title: Once-for-All: Train One Network and Specialize it for Efficient Deployment
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct competitor for selecting compact subnetworks from a shared trained model.
competitive_landscape.difference: Once-for-All trains a supernet supporting depth, width, kernel, and resolution choices and specializes subnetworks for measured hardware. ODN searches only a prefix depth for one dataset and claims simplicity, but provides neither the broader frontier nor a matched total-cost and device comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: Reducing Transformer Depth on Demand with Structured Dropout
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior depth-elastic training method that makes one model robust to post-training layer removal.
competitive_landscape.difference: LayerDrop trains many depth subnetworks through structured dropout and allows depth choice after training. ODN trains a deterministic sequence and yields one chosen prefix; it neither supports arbitrary post-hoc depths nor tests whether progressive expansion improves the accuracy-cost frontier.

competitive_landscape.title: Slimmable Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior once-trained elastic-network method for deployment trade-offs.
competitive_landscape.difference: Slimmable networks share weights across switchable widths and expose multiple accuracy-efficiency operating points. ODN changes depth rather than width and extracts a static prefix, but its evidence does not establish an advantage over a multi-operating-point shared model.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper presents progressive depth expansion as a novel NAS-like procedure that adapts a standard network's depth to dataset complexity and substantially reduces deployment footprint without significant accuracy loss.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The concrete implementation is a warm-up followed by patience-triggered ResNet prefix growth and first-threshold stopping, evaluated on five small classification datasets.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The exact packaging of warm-up, prefix heads, convergence-triggered growth, and target stopping may be distinct, but depth-varying training and reusable subnetworks are well established. Without independent-depth, elastic-network, or search-cost baselines, the supported novelty is a simple heuristic implementation rather than evidence of optimal depth selection or superior efficiency.

reviewer_notes: Read all six extracted pages, including algorithm, tables, plots, conclusion, and references. Competitive records were checked against official arXiv records on 2026-08-23. The strongest qualification is that deployment compression is measured, but search efficiency and optimality are not.
